title: Binary Stars
body:
Most stars come in pairs or larger groups, and a **binary system** is where stellar mass is
measured. Mass cannot be read off a single star's light, so almost every mass in astronomy
traces back to a binary.

Two stars orbit their shared centre of mass. Kepler's third law relates the orbital period and
the separation to the total mass:

$$
M_1 + M_2 = \frac{a^3}{P^2}
$$

in solar masses, astronomical units and years. The ratio of the two orbital radii gives the
ratio of the masses, since the lighter star moves further, and the two equations together give
each mass separately.

Three kinds are observed, distinguished by how the pair is detected:

```
visual        both stars resolved through a telescope
spectroscopic  one spectrum with lines shifting back and forth by the Doppler Effect
eclipsing      the combined brightness dips as one passes in front of the other
```

An eclipsing binary gives more than mass, since the shape and duration of the dip give the
radii of both stars, which is where measured stellar sizes come from.

Binary evolution also produces the exotic objects in the course. A [[White Dwarf]] pulling
material from a companion produces a nova, and enough accumulated mass produces a Type Ia
[[Supernova]], which is the standard candle the distance ladder relies on.
